ancient_source: Albert of Aix, Historia Ierosolimitana; broadly consistent with the order of magnitude given by other First Crusade chroniclers for the combined host at Nicaea
modern_scholar: John France, Victory in the East: A Military History of the First Crusade (Cambridge University Press, 1994)
modern_citation: France, J. (1994). Victory in the East: A Military History of the First Crusade. Cambridge University Press, pp. 122-142.
notes: France reconstructs roughly 4,200-4,500 knights plus around 30,000 infantry as the fighting core, with the 50,000-60,000 range covering the whole host including non-combatants, clergy and camp followers. Notable because the inflation here is the chronicler's OWN side (the Crusader host), not an enemy force, magnifying the scale of Christian mobilisation rather than an enemy threat.

modern_scholar: consensus of modern military historians as summarised in the English Heritage battlefield report
notes: William of Poitiers, writing as chaplain and panegyrist to Duke William, gives 50,000 volunteers assembled for the invasion fleet. No eleventh- or twelfth-century narrative source is considered reliable for troop numbers by modern historians; the modern figure is built from Channel-crossing ship-transport capacity rather than any chronicle count.

modern_scholar: Andrew Ayton and Philip Preston (eds.), The Battle of Crécy, 1346 (Boydell Press, 2005); Clifford J. Rogers
modern_citation: Ayton, A. and Preston, P. (eds.) (2005). The Battle of Crécy, 1346. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
notes: Froissart's figure of 100,000 (other manuscript traditions and an Italian chronicler give as much as 120,000, or a breakdown of 100,000 men-at-arms plus 17,000 infantry/crossbowmen) is rejected by modern historians; French mobilisation financial records do not survive, so the modern figure is a reconstruction from a core of roughly 8,000 mounted men-at-arms plus 2,000-6,000 Genoese crossbowmen plus an unquantified infantry levy. Froissart's own sympathies shifted between English and continental patrons over his career, so side_role is recorded as neutral rather than enemy_of_author.

modern_citation: Rogers, C.J. (2016). 'The Battle of Poitiers, 1356'. Desperta Ferro: Antigua y Medieval, no. 38.
notes: Froissart's 60,000 is the figure generally quoted for the French muster; the modern reconstruction (10,000-12,000 men-at-arms, 2,000 crossbowmen, 2,000 other infantry) is accepted across recent scholarship including Rogers and Sumption. As with Crécy, Froissart's side_role is recorded as neutral given his mixed Anglo-Hainaut-French patronage rather than as enemy_of_author.

ancient_source: later medieval English chronicle tradition building on the Gesta Henrici Quinti (an eyewitness English clerical account that gives the French army as many times the English number without a precise figure); totals as high as 150,000 appear in subsequent English chronicle compilations
modern_scholar: Anne Curry, Agincourt: A New History (Tempus, 2005), arguing for ~12,000, against Juliet Barker, Agincourt: The King, the Campaign, the Battle (Little, Brown, 2005) and Christopher Hibbert, Agincourt (Batsford, 1964), who accept a roughly 3:1 French advantage (~36,000)
modern_citation: Curry, A. (2005). Agincourt: A New History. Stroud: Tempus; Barker, J. (2005). Agincourt: The King, the Campaign, the Battle. London: Little, Brown.
notes: This is a live, unresolved scholarly dispute, not a settled figure. Curry's revisionist ~12,000 (based on French administrative pay records) is disputed by historians who retain a much larger traditional French numerical advantage. modern_figure is the midpoint of the two positions per the project's rule for scholarly disagreement; modern_figure_lo/hi preserve the actual range rather than collapsing the debate onto one side.

ancient_source: contemporary herald's count as reported in a 1461 letter of George Neville, Bishop of Exeter, to Francesco Coppini; Gregory's Chronicle gives an even higher 35,000, while the Neville family chronicler gives a lower 9,000
modern_scholar: George Goodwin, Fatal Colours: Towton 1461 (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 2011), supported by the Towton mass-grave archaeological study
modern_citation: Goodwin, G. (2011). Fatal Colours: Towton 1461. London: Weidenfeld & Nicolson; Fiorato, V., Boylston, A. and Knusel, C. (eds.) (2000). Blood Red Roses: The Archaeology of a Mass Grave from the Battle of Towton AD 1461. Oxford: Oxbow.
notes: Contemporary chroniclers disagree wildly among themselves (9,000 to 35,000), which is itself evidence the 28,000 herald's figure is a rhetorical round number rather than an actual count. Total combatants engaged are also disputed (perhaps 25,000-40,000 across both sides), making a toll of 28,000 dead very hard to sustain; modern reassessment centres closer to 9,000-12,000. Recorded as casualties -- one of at most three such rows in this set.

ancient_source: Annales Gandenses (Annals of Ghent), anonymous Franciscan friar of Ghent, chronicle begun c. 1308
modern_scholar: J.F. Verbruggen, The Battle of the Golden Spurs (Courtrai, 11 July 1302) (Boydell Press, 2002 English translation)
modern_citation: Verbruggen, J.F. (2002). The Battle of the Golden Spurs (Courtrai, 11 July 1302): A Contribution to the History of Flanders' War of Liberation, 1297-1305. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
notes: The same Annales Gandenses passage gives the French cavalry as 'about ten thousand mounted men, besides such a host of crossbowmen and foot that I have not heard their number stated', against a modern French figure of only 2,500-3,000 men-at-arms -- so the French side is comparably inflated but less precisely quantifiable as a total. The Flemish figure is used here because both the chronicle total and Verbruggen's modern total are for the same all-arms infantry force, giving a cleaner like-for-like comparison. This is the chronicler's own side: a Ghent friar writing about the Flemish urban-militia side.

ancient_source: Ottoman order-of-battle document captured from Kara Mustafa Pasha's tent after the battle, dated on or around 10 September 1683 (reporting a decline from 170,000 at the start of the campaign)
modern_scholar: John Stoye, The Siege of Vienna (Collins, 1964)
modern_citation: Stoye, J. (1964). The Siege of Vienna. London: Collins.
notes: This is an Ottoman military-administrative return, not a hostile chronicler's guess, so the gap reflects the normal padding/over-reporting seen in Ottoman campaign musters (which folded large numbers of non-combatant auxiliaries, labourers and irregulars in alongside the fighting establishment) rather than narrative exaggeration by an enemy. European contemporary pamphlets separately claimed figures as high as 300,000; these are not used here since they cannot be tied to a specific named source with the same rigor as the captured muster document.

ancient_source: John, Lord Belasyse, contemporary Royalist officer's account of the campaign
modern_scholar: Glenn Foard, Naseby: The Decisive Campaign (Pryor Publications, 1995), following Sir Bernard de Gomme's contemporary Royalist battle-plan map
modern_citation: Foard, G. (1995). Naseby: The Decisive Campaign. Whitstable: Pryor Publications.
notes: Two contemporary Royalist sources disagree: Belasyse's post-hoc account gives 12,000, apparently inflating the odds his side faced to soften the scale of the defeat, while de Gomme's own battle-plan map (drawn for operational use, not retrospective justification) implies 7,500-9,000 and is preferred by modern historians. A case of own-side inflation motivated by excusing defeat rather than by narrative convention.

ancient_source: Prussian army muster return for the Rossbach campaign, 5 November 1757, as reproduced by Spencer C. Tucker
modern_scholar: Christopher Duffy, Prussia's Glory: Rossbach and Leuthen 1757 (Emperor's Press, 2003)
modern_citation: Duffy, C. (2003). Prussia's Glory: Rossbach and Leuthen 1757. Chicago: Emperor's Press.
notes: By 1757 a Prussian army return survives, and modern historians (Duffy) accept it essentially unchanged: there is no meaningful narrative inflation left to detect on the Prussian side. Included deliberately as a near-zero anchor point for the low-inflation end of the distribution, contrasting with the medieval chronicle cases above. Any small residual variance in this era comes from under-strength companies and detachments left on garrison or escort duty, not rhetorical exaggeration.

side_label: French army under Kellermann engaged at Valmy
ancient_source: contemporary French headquarters report of Kellermann's army strength on the day of the cannonade, 20 September 1792
modern_scholar: T.C.W. Blanning, The French Revolutionary Wars 1787-1802 (Arnold, 1996)
modern_citation: Blanning, T.C.W. (1996). The French Revolutionary Wars 1787-1802. London: Arnold.
notes: Figures here refer specifically to Kellermann's force actually engaged at Valmy on 20 September, not the larger combined French or coalition forces in the wider theatre (Kellermann's and Dumouriez's armies together totalled roughly 54,000, and Brunswick's full coalition army was about 84,000 with only around 34,000 directly engaged). That broader figure is a deployment/scope difference, not source inflation, and is deliberately excluded from this row per the project's guidance on not conflating scope with inflation (cf. the Waterloo warning). The small residual gap recorded here is ordinary reporting variance between the contemporary command estimate and modern reconstruction of the same engaged force.

ancient_source: Austro-Russian allied headquarters strength return for 1-2 December 1805
modern_scholar: David G. Chandler, Austerlitz 1805: Battle of the Three Emperors (Osprey, 1990)
modern_citation: Chandler, D.G. (1990). Austerlitz 1805: Battle of the Three Emperors. London: Osprey.
notes: Modern order-of-battle reconstructions narrow the Allied figure to a 73,200-85,400 range depending on how attached Cossacks and irregular contingents are counted; the contemporary headquarters return sits at the top of that range. A modest, honest reporting gap typical of the staff-return era, not chronicle-style invention -- included as one of the deliberate near-zero anchor cases from 1700 onward.

ancient_source: widely repeated Prussian campaign strength figure for 5 December 1757, as given in general Prussian military historiography
modern_scholar: Christopher Duffy, Prussia's Glory: Rossbach and Leuthen 1757 (Emperor's Press, 2003)
modern_citation: Duffy, C. (2003). Prussia's Glory: Rossbach and Leuthen 1757. Chicago: Emperor's Press.
notes: Duffy's detailed archival reconstruction (33,000) trims the more commonly repeated round figure of 36,000 by roughly 8%, consistent with normal under-strength companies rather than any rhetorical inflation. Paired with Rossbach (same campaign, same author, one month apart) to show two closely spaced, near-zero data points from the same well-documented campaign.
